How America Appeased Putin
item.description:
Excerpt from Spies: The Epic Intelligence War Between East and West

When Spies was first published in 2023, it made front-page news with the chilling revelation that the Russian government had reached an advanced stage in planning an assassination on American soil.

Russia's target was Alexander Poteyev, a former officer in the SVR, Russia's foreign intelligence service, whom the FBI and CIA had recruited as a spy. Poteyev betrayed one of Moscow's most closely guarded secrets: its network of deep-cover "illegals" living in the United States. His intelligence allowed the FBI to arrest ten Russian operatives in 2010, including the glamorous Anna Chapman.

The United States exchanged the illegals for Western agents imprisoned in Russia. Among those released was Sergei Skripal, the former Russian military intelligence officer whom the Kremlin later attempted to murder in Salisbury, England, with the nerve agent Novichok.

The CIA extracted Poteyev from Russia and resettled him under a new identity in the United States. Putin did not hide the fact that he wanted him dead. A Kremlin spokesman warned that Russia knew the traitor's identity and that an assassin would be sent after him.

That was precisely what happened.

Russian intelligence recruited Hector Fuentes, a Mexican microbiologist with a Russian wife and another family in Mexico. His handlers exploited his private life to blackmail him into identifying and surveilling Poteyev in Miami. They gave Fuentes $20,000 to rent an apartment there, but the operation foundered on poor tradecraft. Fuentes photographed the license plate of Poteyev's car and attracted the attention of security guards at Poteyev's apartment complex. When he attempted to leave for Mexico, American border officials discovered the photograph. Fuentes was arrested and disclosed the operation to US investigators.

By authorizing the plot, Putin had crossed an important red line. Europe had already witnessed Russian assassinations and attempted assassinations, including the attack on Skripal. But the Kremlin had previously stopped short of authorising a killing inside the United States. Putin was now demonstrating his willingness to tear up the remaining restraints governing relations with Washington.

Yet the American response was remarkably weak.

The New York Times subsequently reported that Washington retaliated harshly, imposing sanctions and expelling ten Russian intelligence officers operating under diplomatic cover in April 2021. But according to someone intimately involved in the events, when the United States informed the Kremlin about the expulsions, its message did not even mention the planned murder. Instead, Washington concentrated on Russia's SolarWinds cyberattack.

The penalties imposed were hardly sufficient to alter Putin's behaviour. Russian intelligence officers sometimes regard expulsion as a badge of honour. Putin had also insulated much of the Russian economy from American sanctions. A more serious response might have publicly exposed his immense wealth and corruption - subjects about which the Kremlin leader is notoriously sensitive.

The assassination plot was only the first of four events that, viewed from Moscow, advertised American weakness.

The second emerged in 2020, when reports alleged that Russian military intelligence was paying bounties to the Taliban to kill American service personnel in Afghanistan. The story appeared during the presidential election campaign but then largely disappeared, supposedly because the US intelligence community could not reach a consensus about the underlying evidence.

There should have been little doubt. John J. Sullivan, the former American ambassador in Moscow, has written that he examined the intelligence and found the proof persuasive. According to a source with knowledge of the events, American authorities possessed intelligence about a Russian officer travelling to Dubai to meet an Afghan contractor who facilitated payments to the Taliban. At the centre of the scheme was an Afghan-Russian gem smuggler, Rahmatullah Azizi, who acted as an intermediary.

The intelligence reached the President's Daily Brief in February 2020. Donald Trump nevertheless denied having been briefed and dismissed the story as "fake news." As with the assassination plot, the Russian bounty program provoked no meaningful American response.

The third demonstration of weakness was Washington's withdrawal from Afghanistan, negotiated by Trump and executed by Joe Biden in August 2021. The operation was handled disastrously. The world watched desperate Afghans cling to an American C-17 as it taxied along the runway at Kabul airport. Some fell to their deaths after the aircraft took off. A suicide bombing killed thirteen American service personnel and approximately 170 Afghan civilians. Soon the Taliban controlled the country once more.

From the Kremlin's perspective, the images suggested that the United States no longer possessed the will or competence of a superpower.

The fourth episode concerned Havana Syndrome - the mysterious neurological symptoms suffered by American officials since 2016. The US government repeatedly denied that a foreign power was responsible. A 2023 intelligence assessment judged it "very unlikely" that an adversary lay behind the incidents.

Investigative reporting later revealed compelling evidence of Russian involvement. Members of Unit 29155, a Russian military intelligence black-operations squad, were present near several incidents involving American personnel. The operatives appear to have used some form of electronic weapon.

Two reliable sources familiar with the matter told me that Russian involvement was regarded as almost certain, but that elements of the American intelligence community - particularly the CIA - had suppressed evidence pointing towards Moscow. Their apparent calculation was that doing nothing was preferable to revealing an attack that might constitute an act of war.

In December 2024, the House Intelligence Committee concluded that a foreign adversary was increasingly likely to have caused at least some of the incidents. It criticised the previous intelligence assessment for lacking analytic integrity and being highly irregular in its formulation.

If Russia was responsible, the lesson for the Kremlin was unmistakable: it had attacked American government personnel and escaped without punishment.

Taken together, the assassination plot, the bounties on American soldiers, the humiliating withdrawal from Afghanistan and Washington's refusal to confront the evidence surrounding Havana Syndrome all made the United States appear emasculated in the Kremlin's eyes.

It was in this context that Putin decided to launch his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. America appeared weak. The opportunity for military action had arrived.

The analogy with Munich in 1938 has become an overused cliché. In this instance, however, it is unfortunately appropriate. Through their repeated failure to counter Russian aggression before February 2022, the Trump and Biden administrations effectively appeased Putin's worst ambitions.

Putin's actions must be understood through his background as a KGB officer. He remains an unreformed Chekist, steeped in the mentality of the Soviet security services. He has never abandoned the KGB's view of the United States as Russia's "main adversary," nor his conviction that Washington and the CIA are engaged in a conspiracy to weaken Russia.

His strategy has consistently been revanchist: to regain the territory, influence and prestige lost when the Soviet Union collapsed. His invasions of Ukraine in 2014 and 2022 follow logically from that worldview. According to Putin's distorted version of history, Ukraine is an artificial country created by hostile Western powers. He regards its conquest and reincorporation into Russia as an almost sacred duty.

This is a gross misreading of history. But it is nevertheless what Putin believes - and Western governments must take it seriously.

Putin and the hardliners surrounding him believe themselves to be at war with NATO and, above all, with the United States. That conviction will not disappear with a ceasefire in Ukraine. Nor will the danger necessarily vanish when Putin leaves power. The nationalist resentments he has exploited are larger than the man himself, while his regime has systematically eliminated alternative leaders.

The West therefore faces a Russia problem, not merely a Putin problem. The events preceding the invasion of Ukraine offer an enduring warning: deterrence fails when threats carry no consequences. Dictators interpret silence not as prudence, but as permission.

item.title: ‘Coupling without fusion’: Canada and Europe test a new kind of alliance
item.description:
‘Coupling without fusion’: Canada and Europe test a new kind of alliance Expert comment jon.wallace 18 September 2026

The deeper relationship proposed by Carney and von der Leyen could send a powerful geopolitical message. But can agreement be reached without antagonizing EU candidate countries? 

There is something rather extraordinary about the geopolitical times we live in. They are making what seemed impossible yesterday possible today, and what once sounded laughable increasingly credible. This week’s proposals for closer integration between Canada and the EU undoubtedly belongs to that category. 

On 16 September, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada the EU’s first ‘associate member’. The next day, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney used his address to the European Parliament to set out an unusually ambitious programme of economic and strategic integration. 

Canada and Europe, he argued, should cooperate across critical minerals, defence production, artificial intelligence and computing, energy, space and payments. They should move towards ‘seamless’ digital trade in non-agricultural goods and services. And they should expand opportunities for young Canadians and Europeans to live, work and study across the Atlantic. Canada also eyes access to the EU’s Horizon research programme.

If the concept of associate membership is yet to be properly defined – starting with meaningful legal substance – Carney’s address gave it discernible geopolitical purpose. His argument rests on a lesson he has repeated since his Davos speech in January 2026: excessive economic concentration creates vulnerability. And only diversification can restore room for political choice. In Carney’s own words in Strasbourg: ‘The objective is not self-sufficiency. It is collective resilience.’

That logic applies to both sides of the Atlantic. Canada remains extraordinarily exposed to the United States (US), which takes roughly seven in ten Canadian exports. The EU has its own dependencies – including on US technology and security capabilities, Chinese supply chains and, of course, energy imports. 

In this context, both sides of the Atlantic see partnership as a timely opportunity. Seen from Brussels, Canada has much to offer: energy, minerals, Arctic reach, investment capital and advanced capabilities in areas including AI, quantum and space. Seen from Ottawa, the EU also brings a lot to the table: a single market of 450 million consumers, a still strong industrial capacity, world-class research networks and considerable regulatory power.

Want to hear more on the national and economic security intersection in competition policy?

Join us at our competition policy conference to explore how competition policy frameworks are responding to changes in the geopolitical order.

This momentum did not suddenly emerge this week. But the Carney and von der Leyen speeches moved the conversation a step further, giving stronger political expression to a relationship that has been deepening for some time. In June, for instance, Canada became the first non-European country formally brought into procurement under the EU’s €150 billion Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence instrument.  

The relationship is clearly strengthening well beyond trade. It now connects industrial policy, defence production, technology and economic security in ways that the EU has rarely attempted with a non-European power, Japan being probably the closest precedent.

A transatlantic hedge more than a new bloc

Donald Trump’s swift reaction indicates the extent to which the notion of Canadian associate membership really matters. The US president described the prospect as potentially a ‘hostile act’ and threatened heavy tariffs on Europe if Washington concluded that the initiative was directed against the US. Carney responded that Canada would determine its own international partnerships. 

Yet Carney was equally explicit that he is not seeking to construct a rival geopolitical bloc. His proposal might be better understood as an attempt to give countries exposed to great-power economic pressure greater freedom of action. In a way, this model resembles what architects would call ‘coupling without fusion’: two structures that reinforce one another against external pressure but retain their own foundations. 

Canada cannot realistically detach its economy from that of the US. Nor can Europe dispense with the transatlantic security relationship at this stage: the recent trip of the German defence minister to Washington would even indicate the opposite. The purpose here is to reduce specific dependencies on partners like the US while remaining allies.

If it works, the implications could extend well beyond Canada. Von der Leyen has separately proposed a European Security Council involving partners including Canada, Britain, Norway and Ukraine. Carney himself described the Canada–EU arrangement as potentially open to other democracies. All those ideas point towards a looser outer architecture around the EU, where countries participate selectively in European structures without becoming member states. 

In this configuration, the EU would remain the constitutional core of a wider system of concentric circles. Associated countries would be integrated into selected markets, programmes and security structures without acquiring the political rights reserved for members. 

The law has yet to catch up with the politics

Nevertheless, at this stage the ‘associate member’ status remains a political expression rather than a legal category. Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union says that any European state may apply for EU membership. Canada does not meet that geographical requirement.

Creating a formal new category of membership with institutional rights – representation in EU bodies, for example – would therefore require treaty revision. Under Article 48, amendments ultimately require ratification by every member state according to its procedures. That makes genuine constitutional ‘associate membership’ a very ambitious undertaking.

There is, however, an easier route. Article 217 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU does permit agreements with third countries establishing an association based on reciprocal rights and obligations, common action and special procedures. Such association agreements require unanimity in the Council and the consent of the European Parliament. Brussels and Ottawa could therefore deliver most of what Carney envisages without embarking on the long and painstaking journey of treaty revision.

Politically, such an option could suit Canada better. Carney stressed after his speech that sovereignty would be preserved and that any final arrangement would be put to a vote in Canada. He also played down the importance of what Brussels eventually calls it. The difficult negotiations would concern regulatory alignment, market access and reciprocal obligations rather than the ‘nomenclature’.

In Canada, opposition is already visible. Pierre Poilievre’s Conservatives support trade and defence links with Europe but have warned against EU taxation, legislation or free-movement rules applying to Canada. And they argue that Parliament must scrutinize any transfer of authority. 

In Europe, diplomats have questioned what associate membership would mean and noted that von der Leyen’s proposal had not been agreed with the member states beforehand. EU candidate countries could also reasonably ask why Canada should receive privileged access while they undergo years of regulatory and political reform to qualify for membership.

But the immediate warning sign is more tangible. Ten EU member states – including France, Italy, Poland, Belgium and Ireland – have still not ratified the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), nine years after its provisional application began. That unfinished business points towards the political challenges ahead. How likely are EU member states to reach agreement on Canada’s associate membership when a simple free trade agreement struggles to secure full ratification? 

CETA would be the best framework available to provide the commercial foundation of a new Canada–EU association. Defence cooperation through SAFE already offers a template for selective participation in EU instruments. Negotiations would now need to proceed on digital trade, research, student and youth mobility, critical minerals and energy. Institutional arrangements would then gradually build around them.

To borrow an apocryphal line from Lenin, there are decades when nothing happens and weeks when decades happen. These past few days in Strasbourg may come to be remembered as one of those moments when history accelerates.

The EU and Canada are testing how far integration can be achieved between countries that want greater strategic independence without merging their political institutions. Success could have implications far beyond the Atlantic. One conclusion can already be drawn, however: another kind of transatlantic relationship is possible.

World Insights: Mecca defense pact faces first test as Houthi-Saudi tensions intensify
Does Mecca Pact demand Pakistan enter Yemen conflict?
item.description:
In August, the leaders of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed the Mecca Joint Defense Alliance, heralding a new chapter in regional security cooperation between the three nations. In early September, the Houthis launched a new offensive aimed at expanding their control over Yemeni territory and tightening their grip around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Suez Canal and Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.

They subsequently launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia’s military and energy infrastructure on multiple occasions.

As the situation deteriorated, attention increasingly turned to the Mecca Pact and to the question of whether Pakistan would enter the conflict on Saudi Arabia’s side. Some questioned the pact’s credibility, while others argued it was not yet operational. Both interpretations, however, misconstrue the nature of the agreement.

The Mecca Pact establishes the principle that an attack against one member constitutes an attack against all. Yet this does not mean that every drone or missile launched against Saudi Arabia would automatically prompt Pakistan or Turkey to enter the conflict.

NATO offers an instructive parallel. Although Article 5 stipulates that an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all, it requires members to provide “assistance,” not necessarily engaging in an automatic direct military action. Repeated Russian drone incursions into NATO territory, for example, have not automatically triggered Article 5.

Saudi Arabia has not, so far, publicly invoked the Mecca Pact. This reflects an understanding that the pact is intended to provide collective security without outsourcing their primary defense responsibilities to one another. A member that is unable or unwilling to respond to relatively limited attacks on its own could risk creating the free-riding scenario, in which one country relies excessively on allies for its defense.

The member states have an interest in avoiding a situation in which limited attacks become a mechanism for automatically drawing the alliance into a wider conflict. The Middle East already contains multiple overlapping conflicts. If every limited attack produced immediate military intervention by all members, the alliance could rapidly become overstretched. The institutional logic of the Mecca Pact, therefore, favors graduated involvement, with the scale of assistance increasing alongside the severity of the threat.

Pakistan has, nevertheless, made clear that it remains committed to the Mecca Pact. Referring specifically to the conflict in Yemen, Pakistan’s defense minister stated: “We are bound by the terms and conditions of this pact, and we will honor them in case there is a need.”

What many observers overlook is that collective-defense arrangements contain thresholds that determine the form and degree of assistance required at different stages of escalation. Pakistan’s response should, therefore, not be understood in binary terms of intervention or no-intervention.

The more pertinent question is what form of assistance a particular level of escalation would necessitate. The answer could encompass a broad spectrum of military, logistical, intelligence, and diplomatic support.

Diplomacy remains the first instrument for thwarting escalation. Pakistan holds a unique position in this regard. While many states may conduct operations against the Houthis, Pakistan is among the few capable of pressuring Iran to “rein in” the Houthis.

On the military operational side, Pakistan will keep its commitments deliberately ambiguous. There is a strategic rationale for such restraint. Publicly disclosing the circumstances under which members would respond, and the kinds of responses they would make, would allow potential adversaries to tailor their own strategy accordingly. Ambiguity, by contrast, preserves uncertainty over escalation thresholds and can strengthen deterrence. The less an adversary knows about how the alliance would respond, the more difficult it becomes to design a strategy around a predictable reaction map.

Pakistan already has a multi-role military presence in Saudi Arabia, consisting of at least 8,000 troops and 16 aircraft, and “Pakistan will go ‘to any extent’ to defend Saudi Arabia,” as a Pakistani military spokesperson said recently. Operationally, Pakistan can assist and may already be assisting Saudi Arabia in logistics, intelligence sharing and operational management, air defense, and air combat support roles without directly piloting strikes against Houthi sites inside Yemen. Here, Pakistan’s role is, to a certain extent, complementary to Saudi Arabia’s other defense partnerships.

There is a straightforward operational rationale for Pakistan’s current approach.

The Mecca Defense Alliance is a defensive arrangement, not an expeditionary force designed to enable its members to expand their influence beyond their borders. Therefore, Pakistan has little reason to assume a direct strike role in Saudi Arabia’s aerial campaign to thwart Houthi advances inside Yemen, even though those advances are manifestly harmful to Saudi Arabia’s regional interests.

Moreover, the Houthis have not so far generated sufficient operational momentum in their attacks on Saudi Arabia to create an obvious requirement for Pakistani counterforce operations inside Yemen. Saudi Arabia possesses a sizable air force equipped with advanced platforms, including F-15s, to conduct operations inside all of Yemen as it did in its last anti-Houthi campaign from 2015 to 2022. Riyadh, consequently, has the means to conduct precision strikes against the Houthi missile and drone launch positions without requiring a direct combat role for Pakistan.

Pakistan believes this operational dynamic will persist for the foreseeable future.

The situation would change considerably if the Houthis were to launch a large-scale ground offensive into Saudi territory. Such an operation would represent a qualitatively different level of escalation and could trigger a more substantial and direct Pakistani response.

However, in Pakistan’s view, there is currently little military logic for the Houthis to take such an escalatory step. A major ground incursion into Saudi territory would expose Houthi forces to the considerably greater military capacity of Saudi Arabia and potentially of the Mecca Defense Alliance. Rather than improving their strategic position, such an operation could place the Houthis under severe military pressure.

While the operational details and escalation thresholds remain shrouded in ambiguity, there is one thing on which Pakistan’s strategic community agrees: the Houthis should not test the Mecca Defense Alliance.

The strategic importance of Bab el-Mandeb presents a more complicated question. The passage is critical to global trade and energy flows. Saudi Arabia has an especially strong interest in maintaining freedom of navigation in the Red Sea, particularly amid the Hormuz disruption. Pakistan, too, has an interest in securing this critical artery.

Nonetheless, interest in maritime security falls short of justifying an independent Pakistani freedom of navigation operation. Pakistan does not possess the naval capacity to undertake such a mission alone at the scale required to reliably secure Bab al-Mandeb. Any sustained effort to control the passage would also require operations around key coastal areas, including Mokha. Such an undertaking would move well beyond the defensive purpose of the Mecca Pact.

Pakistan’s participation in securing freedom of navigation would, therefore, be more likely if undertaken as part of a broader international coalition. This would provide the operation with a wider legal and political framework, allowing Pakistan to contribute to the protection of a vital international waterway without transforming the Mecca Pact into an instrument for conducting an open-ended military campaign in Yemen.

Of course, the possibility of escalation remains real. Saudi Arabia claims to have shot down a Houthi drone near the holy city of Mecca, a claim that the Houthis deny. Pakistan is deeply committed to countering any threat to the holy sites. As Defense Minister Khawaja Asif said Wednesday, any attack on Mecca or Medina is a “red line” that would draw a Pakistani response even without a mutual-defense agreement. Any Houthi threat in this regard would, therefore, push the conflict several rungs higher on the escalation ladder, giving Islamabad a stronger rationale to intervene directly.

item.title: Why Trump won't 'blow the sh*t out of' Oman today
item.description:
The Sultanate of Oman’s willingness to engage all actors in the Middle East and beyond has long been a pillar of Muscat’s foreign policy. Yet with the war raging in the region, Oman’s efforts to maintain a pragmatic and normal relationship with Iran has fueled friction with the White House.

This was notably underscored by President Donald J. Trump’s earlier threats to “blow up” and “bomb the shit out of” Oman in response to Muscat’s talks with Tehran about the future status of the Strait of Hormuz.

Despite these threats, it is clear that Washington recognizes Oman’s value as a bridge to Iran and other regional actors.

With the struggle for control over Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandab becoming the “Western Front” in the wider U.S.-Iran crisis, the Trump administration has turned to Oman for help with de-escalation efforts and direct talks between Washington and the Ansar Allah movement, better known as the Houthis. On September 15, Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke by phone with his Omani counterpart, Sayyid Badr al-Busaidi, and “expressed support for deepening ties between Oman and the United States,” according to a State Department press release.

“The significance of the Rubio–al-Busaidi call is best understood here in Oman not as an isolated diplomatic courtesy, but as a strong indication that Washington still sees Oman as a necessary diplomatic and strategic interlocutor,” explained a former Omani diplomat who spoke to RS on the condition of anonymity.

“It can be also read as a form of ‘strategic correction’. Whatever the political rhetoric, the U.S. administration needs a functioning relationship with Muscat,” he added.

Several days before Rubio and al-Busaidi spoke by phone, U.S. officials and senior Ansar Allah representatives met at the U.S. embassy in Muscat with support from Omani mediators. During this meeting, which came several days after the Houthis carried out their successful offensive against the forces of the Saudi-backed internationally recognized Yemeni government on the country’s west coast, the Houthis reportedly relayed to U.S. officials that their group has no intention of targeting American vessels.

Meanwhile on September 12, Trump stated that Ansar Allah phoned his administration and asked for Washington to refrain from entering the conflict in Yemen. Two days later, Vice President JD Vance confirmed that Washington was in direct contact with the Houthi movement.

This U.S.-Houthi meeting illustrates how “Muscat is not simply a diplomatic partner in the abstract,” noted the former Omani diplomat. “It is functioning as one of the few places where multiple actors in the regional confrontation can potentially communicate.”

As officials in Muscat see it, instability in Yemen will always threaten Oman’s vital security and economic interests. Conflict in or around the Bab el-Mandab will inevitably disrupt commerce and energy flows. This stands to harm the broader maritime environment, undermining Oman’s ambitions for its ports and logistics hubs, which are key to the country’s Vision 2040 economic development and diversification agenda.

Therefore, preventing an arc of maritime insecurity stretching from Yemen to the Persian Gulf is very much in Oman’s own national interests.

"Despite a relatively neutral foreign policy, Omani officials realize these problems affect them, and when there is something really important in Washington, Oman is willing to help and play a role,” David Des Roches, a professor at the Thayer Marshall Institute, told RS.

Hawkish, neo-conservative organizations, such as Foundation for Defense of Democracies, like to portray Oman as an untrustworthy and problematic actor aligned with the Iran-led camp. But, a U.S. foreign policy that treats Muscat as a threat to Washington’s interests would make it more difficult for the U.S. to pursue its interests vis-à-vis Yemen, the Red Sea, and the Strait of Hormuz.

Rubio’s call with his Omani counterpart “suggests that Washington does not want the U.S.-Oman relationship to become collateral damage in the Iran conflict,” said the former Omani diplomat, who believes that the Trump administration has “realized that a breakdown in U.S.–Oman relations would therefore damage an established American security relationship and potentially eliminate an important diplomatic channel at exactly the moment Washington needs one.”

There is a paradoxical dynamic in play: The ongoing U.S.-Iran crisis makes Muscat’s diplomatic role more valuable at the same time it becomes more potentially dangerous.

“The more Washington needs Oman as an intermediary, the greater Oman’s diplomatic relevance becomes,” said the former Omani diplomat. “But the more Oman becomes involved in U.S.-Iran or U.S.-Houthi diplomacy, the greater the risk that one side interprets Oman’s role as alignment with the other.”

The absurdities of the Trump administration and its hangers-on could be written off as a distraction if the stakes weren’t so high. People might be used to banal trolling on social media platforms, but the global hegemon has forced this petulance onto hundreds of millions of people who are worried about their future and the future of the world. The White House’s online personality is at once extremely disconcerting and extremely juvenile. It’s easy to be stunned by the scale and brazenness of it. item.title: Europe is under attack from three sides – but the EU and Nato are unfit to defend us | Nathalie Tocci
item.description:
Ursula von der Leyen’s outreach to Canada and new security proposals are wise – but she may not be the right messenger

Europe’s strategic predicament is ever clearer, and ever darker. The continent is at war, which is being fought militarily in Ukraine, but is escalating rapidly across Europe through hybrid attacks. Germany’s disclosure that it blames Russia for the explosion at Leipzig airport; a Russian drone strike on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border; an Italian jet shooting down a Russian drone over Lithuania; flares fired from a Russian warship at a Danish helicopter – all within the space of a couple of weeks – tell a coherent story. Whether because Russia is bogged down and unable to advance in Ukraine, or because it believes the US will not come to Europe’s rescue, Vladimir Putin’s regime is ever more bent on escalating its aggression in Europe.

Putin’s calculus is not irrational. Trump never misses a chance to lash out at Europe – the latest example being his threats of further tariffs on the EU if Brussels proceeds to offer Canada “associate membership”. Europeans have grown numb to Trump’s insults and threats, but these threats do underline his deep antipathy, suggesting that if a Russian attack warranted a response, Trump might look the other way. The US certainly can’t be relied on to have Europe’s back.

The Military’s Race to Operationalize AI
item.description:
“I feel as though I was catapulted into a dystopian future in which the battlefield (or ‘kill zone’ as Ukrainians call it) is dominated by drones and sensors, and will increasingly be shaped by AI [Artificial Intelligence], too. It’s where those in command centers digest huge quantities of data to plan operations, allocate drones to target areas, and hunt Russian soldiers and their supplies on myriad computer screens. It’s a type of warfare where the speed of innovation and the ability to scale those innovations are critical assets.”

That was Zanny Minton Beddoes, Editor-in-chief of The Economist, writing last week about a recent trip she and several of her colleagues took to Ukraine, where they were the first foreign journalists to spend a day at the command headquarters of the Nemesis Brigade, one that nation’s top drone units.

She said it felt like being in “a cross between a Silicon Valley startup and a gamers’ gathering,” where, “in the ‘battle room,’ a cavernous space full of banks of monitors and men with consoles, Pavlo Laktionov, the brigade’s deputy commander, explained to me the ‘e-point’ system: The unit can upload video evidence of successful strikes to win points. The value of the Russian target determines the number of points awarded and a leader-board displays which brigade is ahead. He [also] talked me through the way the unit was structured to optimize the speed of speed-back loops between front-line units, the command center, and the brigade’s R&D [research and development] facilities.”

I was fascinated by Beddoes’ modern warfare description coming to me last week at the same time that Air Force Secretary Dr. Troy Meink and Joint Chief Chairman Gen. Dan Caine spoke publicly at an Air & Space Forces Association conference about U.S. gains in developing autonomous warfare capabilities. Meanwhile, I must add, runaway AI has emerged as a new national concern.

When Secretary Meink spoke last Wednesday, most press coverage was directed at his saying, “The United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”

What caught my eye was Meink’s earlier observation: “In the European theater, one-way attack drones have replaced artillery as the primary killer on the battlefield, while armor often sits idle on the side. When I first came into this office, AI really wasn't a commercial thing. Today, it competes with some of the world's top programmers, cyber operators, and hackers. And these technologies are revolutionizing the battlefield.”

He went on to say, “We will be dramatically increasing our combat power by adding large numbers of highly autonomous systems,” and “using novel concepts such as [AI] open systems

architecture to accelerate procurement which has also increased competition from industry resulting in better choices, better prices and in the end more combat power.”

Meink talked about having a significantly different force by 2032, describing “special operators,” not pilots, who will “have the ability to employ thousands of autonomous one-way attack systems, and we will have autonomous fighters like the Collaborative Combat Aircraft or CCAs,” which are un-crewed aircraft powered by jet engines, and potentially equipped for missions including air-to-air combat; air-to-ground combat; electronic warfare; targeting; and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance.

He said, “We intend to have at least 500 of these in service by 2032, and they'll be performing many of the same missions that we do with manned fighters today,” adding, “The first FQ42 and FQ44 increments are already rolling off the assembly line, and I'm excited to name them here for the first time…Fury [FQ-44] and Vengeance [FQ-42].”

Meink pointed out, “These aircraft went from contract award to first flight in 18 months or under; 18 months or under, that's almost unheard of in aircraft development.”

He also said, “And this is not the only class of autonomous aircraft we are aggressively pursuing,” indicating that in the joint U.S.-Israeli Epic Fury, against Iran, “ISR [intelligence surveillance and reconnaissance] strike platforms have been essential.”

“Building on these lessons,” Meink continued, “we are developing a family of low-cost, multi-role, strike platforms called the Mass Modular Aircraft or MMAs [that] will provide affordable attritable [low-cost enough to lose in combat], long-range strike, and we will be able to field them at scale.”

He added, “Our intent is to field 100 MMAs in 2029 at even a lower cost than the CCAs, and a fraction of cost of air-manned aircraft we build today. Then by 2032, 500 of these [unmanned] platforms will join our force operational field fleet.”

Meink also noted, “We are making…progress in our space data network and we are launching our [initial] AMTI [satellites] for our Air Moving Target Indication constellation this month.” AMTI satellites will track airborne threats, such as drones, missiles and aircraft from Low Earth Orbit and replace surveillance aircraft such as the E-3 AWACS. The operational goal is 2028.

“When people look back at this moment,” Meink said, “they will not judge us on whether or not we implemented these autonomous systems, because eventually we're going to. But what we're going to be judged on is how quickly we operationalize them, right? That is whether we operationalize them fast enough to maintain our advantage.”

Meink noted, “We've had autonomous weapons -- I mean whether it's a Tomahawk [long-range, subsonic, precision-guided missile] or any of our air missiles that operate independently at some point in time -- terminal guidance things like that. But the big difference here is really taking

advance advantage of the autonomous capability that the deep-learning [computers] and all these other things [AI] offer.”

He then described having “more autonomy both in the platform as well as in the weapon system itself where even if the weapon loses its outside information stream” but having “enough autonomy to do what we've told it to do in absence of that.”

Reflecting today’s public debate about AI, Meink said, “That's where people start getting nervous, but that is something we have to figure out -- how to get comfortable [with], how to test it, how to verify, certify, that these weapons are going to do what they want when they go into an autonomous mode.”

In his speech last Thursday, Gen. Caine said, “While the fundamental nature of war will always remain the same, a clash of human wills, the character of war, how we fight, the speed at which we fight is changing really, really fast.”

He pointed out, “Information moves so fast that leader decision times has compressed from weeks, down to days, down to seconds. In the future fight, advantage will go to the side who can see first, who can understand first, decide first, and act first -- and along the way be a learning organization. And no factor is accelerating change as fast as Artificial Intelligence and advancing cyber capabilities.”

As Meink had done, Caine said, “AI is here now and it's already changing the way militaries see, sense, decide, and act. And across the joint force, we're putting AI to work every single day to move faster, to make better decisions through active adaptation on every single battlefield by leaders in your joint force.”

As an example, he spoke of what happed last June 8, after a U.S. Army Apache AH64 helicopter on patrol went down near the coast of Oman.

“U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) launched a rapid, responsive, joint search-and-rescue effort to recover the [two-man] crew,” Caine said, adding, “That response drew on the totality of the joint force and ultimately was required to use enabled, unmanned, vessels to participate in the rescue of [the] downed U.S. service members for the first time ever.”

He explained, “That capacity did not appear overnight. It came from the men and women of Task Force 59, CENTCOM's forward-leaning, unmanned, joint maritime unit, who spent the last several years testing, integrating, and operationalizing unmanned systems and AI, in one of the most demanding and kinetic environments on Earth right now.”

Caine added, “What made this possible was a bunch of entrepreneurial sailors and members of

the joint force on watch floors… managing networks of unmanned systems across thousands of miles of water and using AI to turn massive amounts of data into a crisp, clear, perfect maritime picture that allowed us to go grab those two soldiers in the water.”

He then described Ukraine where, he said, “We see first-person-view drones operating in heavily contested [electromagnetic] environments. Some now using AI-enabled computer vision to continue to drive towards targets even when there's no GPS [Global Positioning System] or the [computer] links are cut. That gives small units affordable precision and shows how quickly software and autonomy are changing what is possible at the tactical edge.”

Caine described the stark result: “In certain locations on the front line of troops right now, the life expectancy of a new Russian recruit arriving on the front lines is as little as 20-to-30 minutes. Think about that. This is what happens when low-cost precision is fielded fast, adapted quickly, and scaled across the battlefield.”

“From the Strait of Hormuz to the front lines in Ukraine,” Caine said, “show how quickly technology is changing the character of war…We must move together because the window to build the force that we need is closing. We can buy almost anything in life, but we cannot buy time."

item.title: China is outfoxing the US in the battle for Mideast influence
item.description:
Washington talks about “influence” as though it were a mystical vapor that leaks out of every military base closure. But Beijing’s rapidly growing clout in the Middle East shows that influence can come in many forms.

While the Pentagon debates whether and where to rebuild U.S. bases battered by Iran during Operation Epic Fury, China has spent the last decade expanding its influence in the Middle East without stationing a single soldier there. China’s experience in the region makes clear that influence can be cultivated far more cheaply than Washington assumes, and without maintaining a sprawling network of vulnerable military installations.

As Operation Epic Fury demonstrated, Washington’s constellation of fixed bases across the Middle East is vulnerable and expensive to defend. Before the war, the United States maintained at least 19 military facilities across the region, eight of them considered permanent. Iranian attacks left both the headquarters of the U.S. Fifth Fleet in Bahrain and the Qatar command center, from which the United States had coordinated regional air operations for more than two decades, effectively inoperable.

Defenders of the status quo claim this cost is worth it, arguing that permanent presence keeps Washington politically relevant. Winding it down, they contend, would create a power vacuum to be filled by Beijing, eroding American influence and leaving China as the region’s dominant outside power. China’s own experience in the region invalidates that fear, showing how thoroughly Washington has conflated military power with influence itself.

The Middle East is less strategically important to the United States than it was during the Cold War, and America’s regional interests are correspondingly limited. Washington needs Gulf oil to continue reaching global markets and to prevent any single power from dominating the region and its resources. It also must disrupt terrorist groups capable of striking the homeland.

China’s interests are actually quite similar to America’s. It depends even more heavily on Middle Eastern energy, benefits from a stable balance of power, and has its own concerns about terrorism. Despite these overlapping interests, the two countries have pursued them through starkly different means.

Aside from a single overseas Chinese base in Djibouti, a country where the United States also maintains a base that is roughly six times larger, China has nothing resembling America’s military architecture in the Middle East. Yet Beijing has rapidly expanded its influence in a region where Washington has devoted trillions of dollars and decades of military commitment to the same end.

China enjoys near-universal diplomatic acceptance across the region’s competing camps, while Washington’s history and military entanglements undermine its ability to serve as a neutral mediator. China is the Arab states’ largest trading partner, and the Middle East is one of the largest recipients of its Belt and Road investment. Beijing’s regional diplomatic role has only grown more institutionalized, with the first China-Arab States Summit launched in 2022. Amid the current conflict between the U.S. and Iran, Gulf governments have repeatedly turned to Beijing to pressure Tehran, first over the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian retaliation, and more recently to rein in the Houthis.

Washington remains the region’s preponderant military power, but even that status has not afforded it the ability to dictate the region’s geopolitical alignment. The Gulf monarchies have consistently resisted American efforts to organize the region around great-power competition, instead maintaining close security ties with Washington while deepening relations with China.

While military strength will never be irrelevant, portions of Washington have become so accustomed to exercising power through the military that they often mistake it for power itself. China’s influence has risen alongside its rapid economic growth, technological advances, and growing military capability — the same combination that has built great-power status for centuries. Gulf states sell China the energy its economy depends on while courting Chinese investment because Chinese firms have capital to deploy.

The United States should be great at this game. The Gulf states do not need tens of thousands of American troops on their soil to understand the value of doing business with the world’s largest economy. Nor would America’s decades-old relationships simply evaporate when the last helicopter leaves Saudi Arabia. When Washington is not trying to remake the Middle East in its image, it still has more to offer than Beijing.

Winding down America’s bases in the region would inevitably cost Washington some influence with the countries that host these installations. But influence alone does not make a military presence valuable, especially where the interests at stake are limited. The United States could preserve other forms of security leverage, such as arm sales, capacity building, and intelligence sharing.If anything, some Gulf governments may be more eager to cooperate with the United States knowing they will not be part of a future target set in a regional conflict.

The China-mediated Saudi-Iranian normalization deal in 2023 makes the distinction between military and diplomatic influence clear. Beijing managed to place itself at the center of one of the region’s most bitter rivalries despite lacking anything remotely resembling America’s regional military footprint. It relied instead on diplomacy and the political weight accumulated through its broader relationship with both countries. Influence in the Middle East does not require a military presence, and certainly not one as large as America’s.

There is an even stranger irony in invoking China to justify America’s existing military posture in the region. China depends more heavily than the United States on Middle Eastern energy, yet Washington has effectively appointed itself guardian of the regional order on which China’s economy relies. If Gulf oil flows were ever seriously threatened, Beijing would have every incentive to help restore them. Instead, Washington has saved it the trouble, absorbing all the costs and risks of regional security while China has enjoyed the remarkably convenient arrangement of having its chief geopolitical rival protect its energy lifeline.

As the Pentagon considers what comes next, it should prioritize maintaining regional access rather than regional dominance. It does not need to rebuild every cratered runway or shattered command center simply because those facilities existed before the war.

It should close the most exposed bases, reduce the overall American military footprint, and consolidate what remains around, at most, a few strategic outposts farther from Iran. Jordan, Western Saudi Arabia, the Horn of Africa, or even parts of Europe could still provide the access needed to protect America’s limited regional interests without replicating the sprawling prewar architecture.

Military postures this large are almost impossible to unwind in ordinary times. Operation Epic Fury created a rare chance to break the inertia that keeps outdated deployments alive long after their strategic rationale. The Pentagon should seize it. China is supposed to be the reason America cannot leave; in reality, it provides a clear example of how the United States can protect its interests and preserve its influence at a far lower cost.

item.title: Trump and Xi meet on a 'rotting' diplomatic foundation
item.description:
As Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for his third meeting in less than a year with U.S. President Donald Trump, calm seems to prevail in the relationship. This is a dangerous illusion.

The sense of stability is breeding complacency on both sides even as pressure builds up under the surface. We may be throwing away our last opening to put the world’s most important bilateral relationship on a solid foundation.

In keeping with the slogan on which the two sides agreed at their May meeting in Beijing, the U.S. and China are supposedly building a relationship of “constructive strategic stability.” Indeed, compared to the confrontational posture of both sides during the first Trump and Biden administrations, we seem to have stepped back from the brink of conflict.

Even the seemingly explosive issue of the ongoing U.S. assault against Iran and its damaging consequences for the global economy, or China’s continued dealings with Iran that are frustrating the U.S. strategy of economic strangulation, do not seem to be major grievances for either side.

At first glance, there are strong reasons for rethinking a confrontational approach. In sharp contrast to Biden, Trump does not frame his dealings with Xi Jinping as an ideological crusade. He does not seek to organize the world’s richest and most powerful countries against China or to block its technological development. Trump’s erratic and uninhibited conduct must be deeply disturbing to Xi Jinping, whose dominant psychological trait is an obsession with control. But because Trump wants to strike deals with China rather than geopolitically subordinate it, he has opened a wider range of possibilities in the relationship.

Even more significantly, the U.S. and China find themselves in a balance of economic terror. Last year the relationship nearly spiraled into uncontrollable economic warfare when Trump raised tariffs to 145% in a furious response to China’s retaliation against his “liberation day” tariffs. China then brought to bear its most formidable economic weapon, cutting off U.S. access to the rare earth elements crucial to high tech civilian and military production.

Trump returned to the table in short order, and the two sides deescalated to where they had started. The trade ceasefire was tested five months later when the U.S. Commerce Department imposed a sweeping expansion of its existing blacklist of Chinese companies and China responded by hastily rolling out a much wider version of extraterritorial controls on rare earths. Again furious, Trump threatened to call off the upcoming face-to-face meeting between the two leaders. But when he found out what his administration had done to provoke the Chinese response, he reversed himself.

The economic truce was formalized at the Trump–Xi meeting in Busan, South Korea. Modest progress then followed from Trump’s trip to Beijing in May, with China agreeing to US purchases and both sides promising to talk through ongoing tensions in implementing the truce.

On the surface, then, the relationship seems sound. But underneath, the entire foundation is rotting.

Since 2018, when the US foreign policy establishment abruptly redefined China as alien and hostile to the US-dominated “rules-based international order”, bipartisan hostility toward China has become the single unifying theme in the otherwise floridly dysfunctional US political system. That this unanimity within the political establishment has survived Trump’s second-term reorientation of China policy was on display last week, when multiple congressional hearings were held to denounce China ahead of Xi’s visit. The members of both parties took turns raising antagonistic measures before witnesses chosen to offer only antagonistic approaches to the full range of challenges posed by China.

At a hearing of the House Select Committee on China, for example, Rep. Tom Suozzi (D-NY) asked: “Should we be viewing this as a hawkish relationship between us and China? … Or should we be doing more of a cooperative relationship with them—because we tried that for like 50 years ever since Nixon went to China, and that didn't turn out very well for us.”

The Republican and Democratic witnesses alike agreed that the key task is to slow down China’s economic and technological development and speed up that of the United States. In the words of witness Oren Cass, “it should be extremely obvious to us that there is no path to partnership, collaboration, mutually beneficial arrangements with China.”

To the limited extent that Trump’s administration is making China policy, it is guided by the same sort of hostility. Although Trump’s desire for friendly meetings with Xi Jinping has starkly limited public anti-China rhetoric and has hamstrung the Commerce Department after its actions nearly derailed the Busan summit, other U.S. agencies are continuing the Biden practice of steadily expanding restrictions on China:

— The Federal Communications Commission has banned the import of humanoid robots and power inverters from China and expanded the ban on imports from Huawei and ZTE.

— Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy recently sent a letter to Ford denouncing the automaker’s agreements with Chinese companies for creating “reliance on technologies of foreign adversaries”.

— Under a proposed rule set to take effect in December, the Office of Management and Budget would prohibit federally funded US research collaboration with Chinese researchers.

— The Pentagon keeps expanding its own blacklist of Chinese entities, and has now included most of China’s leading private technology companies.

— Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, commenting recently on the artificial intelligence “race” that US leaders imagine themselves to be running against China, said: “There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this.” Trump himself holds the same view. (After talks on Sunday with his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng, Bessent said the two sides had agreed to establish an AI dialogue mechanism. This is an encouraging sign, but the atmosphere of deep distrust over technology will make real progress on the issue difficult.)

Washington may be split, then, on how to talk about China. But on the substance of the relationship, overwhelming agreement prevails: U.S. and Chinese interests are inalterably opposed, the U.S. must dominate China or lose itself, excluding China’s presence in American society is an urgent priority.

Because China is expanding its own capacity to counter U.S. attacks, and because neither side seems to understand what the other has promised in their truce, the two countries are headed for turmoil if not outright conflict.

U.S. policymakers could still step back from such a mutually destructive future. The American people are communicating quite clearly that they do not want the single-mindedly adversarial approach that Washington has embraced. A clear majority now favor cooperation with China rather than seeking to limit its power.

Recognizing the many shared interests that do unite the U.S. and China could open possibilities for cooperation on urgently needed global reforms. Appreciating the deep economic changes on both sides over the last decade would allow the two countries to explore different possibilities for mutual gain in trade and investment and research collaboration. New thinking on AI would make both countries safer and more prosperous. Taking seriously the idea of “constructive strategic stability” could inspire a new approach to regional security.

Policy ideas for repairing the relationship are available. What is in short supply are U.S. leaders with the political courage to stand against the latest ill-fated bipartisan demand for international conflict.

item.title: When Saudi Arabia realizes it's backed the wrong horse
item.description:
The United States went to war with Iran in the belief that American power could quickly overwhelm Tehran’s ability to threaten the Middle East. For Saudi Arabia, the war is producing nearly the opposite result.

Iran has been badly hit, but it and its regional allies have demonstrated that they can still threaten Saudi cities, oil installations, pipelines and export routes. At the same time, Washington has shown that even overwhelming offensive power does not necessarily translate into effective protection for its Gulf partners. The consequence is likely to be a historic Saudi reassessment: less confidence in the United States, more reliance on regional partners and a much closer strategic relationship with China.

Saudi Arabia’s geographical problem is not new. In an article published in LobeLog in September 2019, I described the “encirclement” of Saudi oil production by Iran and Iran-aligned forces. That year, the attack on the Abqaiq processing complex displayed the accuracy and reach of the weapons available to Tehran or its allies. An earlier Houthi strike on pumping stations serving the East-West Pipeline showed that the kingdom’s alternative export route to the Red Sea was also vulnerable. Attacks around Fujairah similarly cast doubt on the idea that tankers and pipelines outside the Strait of Hormuz would remain safe in a crisis.

The strategic message was straightforward. Saudi Arabia could not protect its petroleum system simply by building routes that bypassed one chokepoint. Its fields and processing plants lie near the Gulf; the East-West Pipeline crosses a vast, exposed territory; and the Red Sea outlet can be threatened from Yemen. Iran’s influence in Iraq, Syria, Lebanon and Yemen gave it the ability to apply pressure around much of the kingdom’s perimeter.

In 2019, Saudi leaders were deeply disappointed when the United States did not retaliate against Iran for the attack on Abqaiq. They had invested heavily in their relationship with the first Trump administration. Later, the Saudi Public Investment Fund’s $2 billion commitment to Jared Kushner’s private-equity firm reinforced the impression that Riyadh expected its close connections to the Trump family to bring privileged access and dependable support. Whatever the Saudis expected, Abqaiq had already demonstrated the limits of the American security guarantee.

The present war makes that problem much greater. The United States can destroy targets across Iran, but it has not been able to prevent Tehran and its partners from striking back across the region. Saudi Arabia is now paying for a conflict it did not start and cannot control. Missile and drone defenses can intercept many threats, but no shield is perfect, particularly against repeated, low-cost attacks on sprawling infrastructure.

Recent strikes on the East-West Pipeline underline the point made in 2019: the route intended to insure Saudi exports against the closure of Hormuz is itself a target. The kingdom is surrounded not by conventional Iranian armies but by a network of missiles, drones, militias and maritime threats.

For Riyadh, therefore, the issue is not simply the strength of the U.S. military. It is the mismatch between American power and Saudi security. Washington may be able to punish Iran severely without being able to stop attacks on Abqaiq, Ras Tanura, Yanbu or the pipeline between them. Indeed, a prolonged war can increase those attacks by giving Iran an incentive to raise the cost to America’s partners. Saudi Arabia is likely to be even more angered by the ineffectiveness of American protection now than it was by American restraint in 2019.

The deterioration extends beyond immediate defense. The U.S.–Saudi civil nuclear agreement once appeared to be the centerpiece of a broader strategic bargain. Yet after supporting the agreement, President Trump publicly made its political future dependent on Saudi participation in the Abraham Accords. That demand is extraordinarily difficult for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to meet while Israel continues its operations in Gaza, expands pressure in the West Bank and wages war in southern Lebanon. The agreement has been submitted to Congress and is not formally dead but tying it to normalization has placed it in severe political jeopardy.

From Riyadh’s perspective, Washington has again turned a promised strategic benefit into a conditional instrument of American and Israeli policy.

Saudi leaders must now ask whether they have been backing the wrong horse. Their answer is not likely to be a complete break with Washington. The United States will remain an important arms supplier, investor and military partner. But the kingdom is already building alternatives.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed in August by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey commits the three countries to treat an attack on one as an attack on all. Its practical obligations remain to be tested, yet its political meaning is clear. Saudi Arabia no longer wants its survival to depend on a single outside protector. Pakistan offers nuclear prestige and a long military relationship; Turkey brings a capable defense industry, armed forces and NATO experience. Together, they provide Riyadh with an additional layer of deterrence and strategic autonomy.

China is the more consequential alternative. It is the largest buyer of Gulf oil, an indispensable economic partner for Saudi development and one of the few powers with real leverage in Tehran. Beijing also brokered the 2023 restoration of Saudi-Iranian diplomatic relations. Unlike Washington, China does not ask Riyadh to normalize relations with Israel or align itself publicly with a divisive regional war. Saudi leaders may increasingly conclude that China, precisely because it maintains relations with both sides, is better placed to restrain Iran and protect the commercial stability on which the kingdom depends.

That does not mean China will replace the United States as Saudi Arabia’s military protector. Beijing has neither America’s regional force structure nor an evident desire to inherit its security burdens. But influence does not require exact replacement. China can supply digital and nuclear technology, investment, diplomatic access and eventually more defense cooperation, while Saudi Arabia assembles a diversified security system involving Washington, Beijing, Islamabad and Ankara. Each disappointment with the United States accelerates that process.

The great irony is that an American war intended to reassert U.S. power may instead reduce U.S. primacy in the Gulf. President George W. Bush’s invasion of Iraq removed Iran’s principal Arab counterweight and handed Tehran enormous influence in Baghdad. President Trump’s war with Iran risks a comparable strategic reversal. By exposing Saudi Arabia to retaliation, demonstrating the limits of American protection and attaching unacceptable political conditions to cooperation, Washington is encouraging Riyadh to seek security elsewhere.

Bush’s war helped hand Iraq to Iran. Trump’s war may help hand the Gulf—and above all Saudi Arabia—to China.

In the preface to volume one, “The Gathering Storm,” of his six-volume memoir of World War II, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill recalls a conversation with U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt, in which Roosevelt asked what the war should be called. Churchill responded instantly, “the unnecessary war,” noting that it was the easiest war to stop. The world is now at war in Europe and the Middle East and at risk of escalation that could become a world war. This escalation is unnecessary and could be stopped by relearning some of the lessons that led to the Second World War.

French President Macron called a meeting of French political leaders on Friday to receive briefings on the changing and more aggressive nature of Russian hybrid attacks against European states, citing the attempted explosives-laden drone attack against Leipzig airport. Macron also announced an upcoming G7 meeting to address energy security and joint measures to address Russian airspace violations, surveillance of defense sites, maritime meddling, and sabotage and assassination operations. Macron’s concerns reflect assessments in 2026 by the intelligence services of the Baltic States as well as Sweden and Finland that Russia is planning a provocation against a NATO state in the near term. These assessments, as well as information gathered by U.S. intelligence, may have contributed to the decision by the U.S. to send CIA Director Ratcliffe to Moscow to warn President Putin against such a provocation.

Putin intends to bring the war to the U.S. The September 15 indictments of five operatives linked to a Russian intelligence network in the U.S. for conspiring to finance terrorism and orchestrate a murder-for-hire plot against a Russian dissident in the U.S. may have been a bit of a wake-up call in Washington that the type of hybrid “grey zone” operations Europe has experienced from Russian intelligence in recent years is heading to the U.S. This should come as no surprise. To Putin, the U.S. is the “main enemy,” and anything to weaken the ability or willingness of the main enemy to stay in the fight is certain to be a key part of Putin’s escalation strategy. Messaging to Moscow is important, and President Trump should no longer be under any illusions about the nature of his relationship with the Russian dictator. Putin is his enemy.

President Trump’s choice of negotiators to send to Moscow to try and reach a negotiated solution to the conflict could not have been more poorly chosen. The Kushner-Witkoff team should not have been used to deliver the message Ratcliffe delivered because they do not have the standing or credibility in Moscow’s eyes. Witkoff’s sad gushing about the history of the moment and his memories of Putin are sad and embarrassing. More importantly, though, they deliver exactly the wrong message to Putin. Putin doesn’t respect flattery from characters like Kushner and Witkoff. Putin’s choice of their principal interlocutor from the Russian side, Kirill Dmitriev—the CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund—shows that Putin has assessed accurately the real motivation of the Kushner-Witkoff team: business deals and money.

There is a reason for sending the CIA Director to deliver different messages. One might recall the visit of then-CIA Director Burns to Moscow in 2021 to warn Putin against again invading Ukraine. Burns clearly delivered a message based on intelligence information on Russian plans and intentions—which proved correct—and I suspect Ratcliffe delivered the same type of message based on similar intelligence. Using CIA Directors to deliver such messages is important because Putin mirror-images. He trusts information from his intelligence and security services far more than information from his Ministry of Foreign Affairs or other sources. If the information carried to Moscow comes from the CIA Director, it, by definition, has more credibility than information from any other source. This doesn’t mean Putin will heed the message, but it will reach his ear. But the key to the efficacy of messages delivered by CIA Directors is the credibility of consequences. Clearly, Putin correctly assessed that the consequences he would face from President Biden for invading Ukraine in February 2022 would be gradual and, in the end, inconsequential. He may believe the same will be the case with the Trump/Ratcliffe messaging.

If it hasn’t been clear for years, it should be absolutely clear now: Putin is all in on this war. There is no indication from Moscow of any change in Putin’s absolutist terms for ending the war. Putin cannot negotiate a peace short of capitulation by Kyiv. Ending the war short of Putin’s definition of victory risks a disgruntled army returning to Moscow, and history is not kind to Russia’s leaders in such a scenario. Perhaps as important, ending the war short of victory leaves Russia in a much worse strategic situation with Ukraine’s emergence as the preeminent military power in central Europe. Germany and the EU are rearming. NATO membership has increased with the addition of Sweden and Finland. Russia’s economy is in tatters as a result of sanctions and Ukrainian strikes against energy, military, and military support infrastructure deep in the territory of the Russian Federation. The war cannot be hidden from the Russian people any longer. The pressure of his handling of the war may possibly be starting to take a toll on Putin himself. His performance at the Navy Day celebration in St. Petersburg this July, where for the second consecutive year the parade of warships was cancelled and Putin’s appearance was indoors in front of a poster of a Russian submarine, was widely ridiculed. The city was essentially on lockdown for security reasons. Putin followed the widely ridiculed appearance in St. Petersburg with a highly staged visit to Russia’s Far East that was received locally with widespread cynicism but included a first visit to Iturup Island, triggering strong criticism from Japan but serving as a symbol of Putin’s determination to keep and increase the boundaries of the Russian Federation.

Putin’s determination and perhaps conviction that he is on a path to victory belies objective analysis of the war against Ukraine and Russia’s economic and strategic situation. Putin’s determination is likely reinforced by the approach the Trump Administration has taken, accommodating Moscow and putting pressure on the victim. This may be starting to change, and perhaps President Trump is starting to realize that Putin is his enemy, the enemy of the United States and the West, and a supporter of Iran—currently engaged in active military activity to kill Americans and wreck energy markets (among other markets) to undermine Western economies.

Trump signed the long-delayed sanctions legislation sponsored by the late Senator Lindsey Graham. This legislation allows for primary and secondary sanctions on Russia and other countries by allowing tariffs on the largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas and the top five countries that aid Russia’s energy sanctions evasion. There has been a suggestion that officials in the Trump Administration are trying to create more incentives for members of the Russian elite to seek peace. If true, this is an interesting change in the Administration’s approach, which has thus far been to ingratiate itself to Putin. Putin seems highly resistant to pressure from outside the Russian Federation, and there is no level of economic hardship or war casualties Putin is unwilling to inflict on the docile Russian population. His latitude to resist pressure from disenfranchised or recently relatively impoverished Russian elites may be less so.

There is a path to making the coming war unnecessary. The key to the problem is Putin. He is at the center of the spider’s web of the cabal acting against the free world. Iran, its surrogates, principally the Houthis at the moment, China, and North Korea are key pieces in Putin’s architecture of disruption. To destroy this architecture, you have to destroy its architect. Defeat Putin in Ukraine, and Iran’s position in the Middle East will surely erode, and a powerful message will have been sent to Chinese President Xi to keep his hands off Taiwan.

Unlike Churchill and Roosevelt at the onset of World War II, the free world has a valiant and effective military partner eroding Putin’s power: Ukraine. Therefore, the first step in deterring the coming unnecessary war is to provide Ukraine the military and financial support it needs to win. This starts with air defense to protect against Putin’s increasing use of modified drones and ballistic missiles to target Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and civilians in an attempt to erode Ukrainian willingness to resist—a problem which could become more acute as winter approaches.

Secondly, Ukraine should be encouraged to continue its effective targeting of Russian energy, economic, and military infrastructure, which is helping to erode support within Russia for Putin’s regime and his war of aggression. Ukraine should be encouraged and given the support it needs to continue its current offensive northeast of Lyman in the Donetsk Oblast. Ukraine should be encouraged to engage in operations to liberate Crimea, which is the jewel in the crown of Putin’s territorial “achievements.”

It would be well worth the effort of the U.S. and the West to put pressure on Russia’s periphery, starting with enhancing support for pro-Western elements in the Republic of Georgia—long an outlier of Western support in the Caucasus and itself a victim of Putin’s aggression in August 2008 and currently under pressure from pro-Russian elements supported by Russia’s intelligence services. The U.S. decision to deploy forces to Poland and NATO’s decision to deploy more forces to the Baltic States are another useful way to stretch Putin’s resources and pressure him.

The lessons of history are clear: appeasement of aggression brings more aggression. Strength and resolve are the key to avoiding unnecessary wars. It is time the Trump Administration learned history.

item.title: In UN speech, Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal reached
item.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump threatened Tuesday to “annihilate” Iran if diplomatic efforts to end his nearly seven-month-old war do not succeed. Speaking to the United Nations General Assembly, he also touted both his peacemaking record and an increasingly belligerent U.S. foreign policy stretching from the Middle East to Venezuela to Greenland.

Trump presented the past year as proof that military force and economic pressure could resolve conflicts that diplomacy had failed to settle.

“As president of the most extraordinary nation in history, I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day,” he declared. “I do not believe in letting problems fester; they only become harder to solve. So while others have talked, I have acted.”

The leading example of this approach, Trump said, was Iran, which, in his telling, has rejected Washington’s diplomatic overtures that had pushed Trump to take military action with Israel in June 2025 and then launch a much larger-scale war beginning at the end of February.

“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said of the current status of the war. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before (...) Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly?”

Trump has made several similarly dark threats against Iran during the conflict, but they have done little to alter Tehran’s negotiating position, and the two sides appear stuck in a standoff, with some fearing that the operation is doomed to become another American “forever war”.

The president, however, predicted that the two sides will reach an agreement after November’s midterm elections, because “it doesn't make sense for” Iran not to.

“They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election, what they don't realize is that I'm not running,” he added, saying that national security questions, not political considerations will drive his calculus. But the war does seem to be affecting the president’s popularity. A recent poll by CNN shows that opposition to Trump’s approach to the war continues to grow, with only 26% saying that they support the president’s approach, and nearly 80% saying he is not doing enough to bring the war to an end.

Trump blasted the “cowards and traitors” who say that U.S. munitions stockpiles are dwindling to a dangerous extent. The Congressional Budget Office recently found that it could take five years to replenish them.

Elsewhere, Trump said he would “continue to seek and end the disastrous war between Russia and Ukraine,” while threatening to use the “enormous” new tariff authorities granted to him by the Russia sanctions package that passed Congress last week. He also said that he would sign the recently announced deal with Denmark and Greenland that would increase the U.S. military presence in Greenland later Tuesday.

Trump closed his remarks by downplaying the growing worries over artificial intelligence’s threat to humanity, instead presenting the race to “superintelligence” as part of a competition with China.

“Whoever wins superintelligent wins,” he said. “That's the group that wins, and we're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way.”
